name: AI for Restaurants
objectives: Given the real ingredients and method for a dish, write a short menu description with AI help and remove anything that is not true, with every ingredient word matching your recipe

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Menu, allergens and kitchen lists

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing menu descriptions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write short, mouth-watering and accurate menu descriptions with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Given the real ingredients and method for a dish, you will write a short menu description with AI help and remove anything that is not true, with every ingredient word matching your recipe.
A good menu description says what is in the dish, how it is cooked, and why it is special, in 10 to 25 words. "Jollof rice slow-cooked in tomato and pepper sauce, served with fried plantain and grilled chicken thigh."
Give AI the real ingredients and method: "Write a 20-word menu description for: goat curry, bone-in, slow-cooked 4 hours with scotch bonnet, thyme and potatoes, served with white rice. Warm, simple words." Ask for three versions and pick one.
Check it. AI may add ingredients you do not use ("with cashews") or words like "organic" or "house-made" that are not true. A wrong ingredient on a menu can hurt someone with an allergy.
Step by step:
- Write the real ingredients and cooking method.
- Ask AI for three short descriptions.
- Pick one and check every ingredient word.
- Remove anything not true, like "organic".
Words to know:
- Menu description: the short text under a dish name that tells guests what it is.
Try it now: Write menu descriptions for five of your dishes with AI help. Check every ingredient word against your recipe.
You can now write accurate, appealing menu descriptions with AI help.

check.q: What three things does a good menu description say?
options: What is in the dish, how it is cooked, and why it is special
The price, the cook's name and the plate size
The calories, the supplier and the date
Only the name of the dish in capital letters
check.why: The lesson says a good description covers what is in it, how it is cooked and why it is special.

check.q: AI writes "house-made organic tortillas" but you buy regular tortillas. What do you do?
options: Keep it because it sounds better
Remove "house-made" and "organic" because they are not true
Add more words like "artisan"
Ask AI to write it in capital letters
check.why: Menu words must be true, so you remove anything AI added that you do not do.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building an allergen chart, safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build an allergen chart from your own recipes and labels, checked by you.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own recipes and the labels of what you buy, you will build an allergen chart that marks the FDA's nine major allergens for each dish, with every dish checked by a second person.
The FDA lists nine major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Guests with allergies rely on you to know what is in each dish.
Make a chart: dishes down the side, the nine allergens across the top. Fill it from your actual recipes AND the ingredient labels of everything you buy, because sauces, spice mixes and breads often hide allergens. AI can help you set up the table and remind you which ingredients commonly contain an allergen, but it does not know your suppliers' products. You and your labels do.
Update the chart whenever a recipe or supplier changes. Train staff to say "Let me check" and ask the kitchen, never guess. Your local health department and the FDA Food Code have rules on food safety and allergen awareness; check what applies where you are.
Step by step:
- List your dishes and every ingredient in each.
- Read the label of each bought ingredient.
- Mark each of the nine allergens per dish.
- Have a second person check the chart.
- Update it when recipes or suppliers change.
Words to know:
- Allergen: a food that can cause a serious allergic reaction in some people.
- Cross-contact: when an allergen gets into another food by shared surfaces, oil or tools.
- Food Code: the FDA's model food safety rules that many states and counties adopt.
Official sources:
- FDA: Food Allergies (the nine major food allergens)
- FDA: Food Code
Try it now: Ask AI to set up an empty allergen chart for five dishes with the nine allergens as columns. Fill it in yourself from your recipes and ingredient labels, then have someone check it.
You can now build and maintain an allergen chart from your own recipes and labels.

check.q: What goes across the top of the allergen chart in this lesson?
options: Your prices
Your suppliers' names
The nine major allergens
Your staff's names
check.why: Dishes go down the side and the nine allergens go across the top.

check.q: Your supplier changes the brand of spice mix you use. What do you do?
options: Nothing, spice mixes never have allergens
Ask AI if the new brand has allergens and trust it
Wait until a guest asks
Read the new label and update the chart
check.why: AI does not know your suppliers' products; you update the chart from the new label.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Prep lists and order lists from your sales
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a weekly prep list and order list from your sales numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Given your average sales per day and portions per batch, you will create a weekly prep list and order list in a spreadsheet, with batches rounded up and adjusted for events, weekends and weather.
Over-prepping wastes food; under-prepping means "sorry, we're out". Start with how many of each dish you sell per day. Your POS can often show this, or keep a simple tally.
In a spreadsheet: Dish, Average sold per day, Portions per batch, Batches needed. Then list the ingredients per portion to see what to order. Ask AI for help with the formulas: "Write a Google Sheets formula to round up batches needed: average sold divided by portions per batch." (=ROUNDUP(B2/C2,0) is one way.)
Adjust for what you know: weekends, events, weather, holidays. AI can suggest a prep list layout and a checklist, but your numbers and experience set the amounts.
Step by step:
- Get average sold per day for each dish.
- Add portions per batch and calculate batches with ROUNDUP.
- List ingredients per portion and total the order.
- Adjust for weekends, events and weather.
Words to know:
- Prep list: a list of what the kitchen must prepare before service.
- Par level: the amount of an item you want on hand at the start of service.
- Batch: one cooking of a recipe that makes a set number of portions.
Try it now: Make a prep sheet for five dishes with sold-per-day, portions per batch and a ROUNDUP formula for batches. Turn it into an order list for one week.
You can now build prep and order lists from your own sales numbers.

options: Wasted food
Running out of a dish
Longer opening hours
Higher rent
check.why: The lesson says over-prepping wastes food and under-prepping means running out.

check.q: A big festival is in town this weekend. What do you do with your prep list?
options: Use the usual numbers exactly
Adjust the amounts up based on what you know
Let AI set the amounts with no changes
Stop making a prep list
check.why: You adjust for events, weekends and weather, because your experience sets the amounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drafting a staff schedule
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a weekly schedule with AI help, then check it against your rules.
This lesson builds toward: Given your hours, shifts and workers' first names and availability, you will draft a weekly staff schedule with AI and check it for coverage, fairness and labor rules, with no private worker details in the prompt.
Give AI the facts: your hours, how many people you need each shift, each worker's availability and roles, and your rules. "Draft a weekly schedule for my taqueria, open 11-9 Tuesday-Sunday. Need 2 cooks and 2 front staff at lunch and dinner. Here are availabilities: [first names only]."
Check the draft yourself. Make sure it is fair, covers busy times, and follows labor laws on breaks, overtime and minors. Those rules depend on your state and city; check your state labor department or a professional. AI does not know them reliably.
Do not put Social Security numbers, pay rates with names or private notes about workers into AI tools. First names and availability are enough.
Step by step:
- List shifts and people needed.
- List workers by first name with availability and roles.
- Ask AI for a draft.
- Check fairness, coverage and labor rules for your state.
- Post the final schedule.
Words to know:
- Availability: the days and times a worker can work.
- Overtime: extra hours that may require higher pay under labor law.
- Coverage: having enough staff on each shift.
Try it now: Draft next week's schedule with AI using first names and availability. Check coverage and fairness, and write where you will check your state's break and overtime rules.
You can now draft a staff schedule with AI and check it against your own needs and labor rules.

check.q: What facts does AI need to draft a schedule?
options: Workers' Social Security numbers and pay
Only the restaurant's name
Your hours, people needed per shift, and workers' availability and roles
Private notes about each worker
check.why: Hours, shift needs, availability and roles are enough; private details stay out.

check.q: AI's draft schedules a 16-year-old on a late shift. What do you do?
options: Post it as it is
Ask AI if it is legal and trust the answer
Remove the worker from the schedule forever
Check your state's rules for minors and fix the draft
check.why: Rules on minors depend on your state, so you check them and fix the schedule yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Answering reviews and guest messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Reply to reviews and common guest questions quickly and honestly.
This lesson builds toward: Given a guest question or a good or bad review, you will write a calm, honest reply with AI help, with every statement true and no fake or paid-for reviews.
Guests ask the same things: hours, parking, reservations, catering, vegan options, allergies. Use AI to turn your real answers into short replies you can paste. For allergy questions, always point to your checked allergen chart and staff.
For reviews: thank good reviews briefly and mention the dish. For bad ones, stay calm, apologize for the experience, say what you are fixing, and invite them to contact you. Do not argue publicly. Let AI draft a calm version if you are upset, then check every statement is true.
Never write fake reviews or pay only for positive ones. The FTC's rule on consumer reviews bans this, including AI-written fakes.
Step by step:
- Write real answers to your top guest questions.
- Ask AI to make short paste-ready replies.
- Draft review replies calmly with AI, then check them.
- Never fake or buy reviews.
Words to know:
- Review: a guest's public rating and comment.
- Catering: providing food for an event outside the normal dine-in service.
Official sources:
- FTC: Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule, Questions and Answers
Try it now: Ask AI to draft replies to one good and one bad review (real or sample, such as cold food on a busy Friday). Make every statement true and in your voice.
You can now answer guest questions and reviews quickly, calmly and honestly.

check.q: How should you answer a good review?
options: Thank them briefly and mention the dish
Ignore it
Offer them money for another review
Write a long story about your restaurant
check.why: The lesson says to thank good reviews briefly and mention the dish.

check.q: You are angry about an unfair bad review. What do you do?
options: Argue with the guest in public
Let AI draft a calm reply, then check every statement is true
Post fake good reviews to hide it
Delete your business page
check.why: AI can help you stay calm, and you check the reply is true; you never argue publicly or fake reviews.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Planning specials that use what you have
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a weekly special that cuts waste and keeps a profit.
This lesson builds toward: Given extra or seasonal ingredients, you will plan a weekly special, calculate its plate cost and set a price with a profit, with allergens checked and the special added to the prep list.
Specials can sell extra stock before it spoils, test new dishes and bring regulars back. Look at what you over-ordered or what is in season.
Ask AI: "I have extra plantains, black beans and chicken thighs this week. Suggest three specials that fit my Caribbean menu and use mostly these." Pick one, cost it out (ingredients per plate), and set a price with a profit.
Write the special's description, check its allergens against your chart method, add it to your prep list, and post it with a photo of the real dish.
Step by step:
- List extra or seasonal ingredients.
- Ask AI for special ideas that fit your menu.
- Cost the plate and set a price with profit.
- Check allergens and add to the prep list.
- Post with a real photo.
Words to know:
- Plate cost: the cost of the ingredients in one serving.
- Food cost percentage: plate cost divided by menu price, times 100.
Try it now: Final task: build your restaurant kit: five menu descriptions, an allergen chart from your recipes and labels, a week's prep and order lists, a draft schedule, two review replies, and one special with its plate cost.
You can now use AI across your restaurant's planning, paperwork and guest communication, safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Accurate menu descriptions A description lists an ingredient or claim that is not in the dish. Five short descriptions, every ingredient word matching the recipe. Each one also says how the dish is cooked and why it is special. Checked allergen chart The chart is copied from AI or missing a dish or allergen. All five dishes marked for the nine allergens from recipes and labels, checked by a second person. Notes which bought items hide allergens and when the chart was last updated. Prep and order lists Amounts are guessed or batches are not rounded up. A week's prep and order lists built from sales with batches rounded up. Amounts are adjusted for a named event, weekend or weather. Fair, checked schedule The schedule leaves a busy shift short or used private worker details. Covers every shift fairly, uses first names only, and notes where labor rules were checked. Also notes breaks and any rules for minors from the state source. Honest review replies A reply argues, makes a false promise or offers a reward for reviews. One good and one bad review answered calmly with only true statements. The bad-review reply names a real fix and invites the guest to make contact. Costed special The special has no plate cost or price. One special with plate cost, a price with profit, and allergens checked. Also added to the prep list and uses extra or seasonal stock. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is one reason to run a special?
options: To raise prices on everything
To use up staff hours
To sell extra stock before it spoils
To avoid checking allergens
check.why: Specials can sell extra stock, test new dishes and bring regulars back.

check.q: AI suggests three specials from your extra plantains. What do you do next?
options: Post all three right away with stock photos
Ask AI to set the price
Skip costing because it is only for one week
Pick one, cost the plate and set a price with a profit
check.why: You cost the plate and price it for a profit, then check allergens and add it to the prep list.
